text: Metritis/vulval discharge: clear discharge is normal during estrus or shortly after delivery, but pus in the discharge signals uterine infection (endometritis). The uterus is normally sterile; it gets contaminated with vaginal microbes right after delivery but normally clears them within days — sometimes infection persists instead (from retained placenta, hormonal issues, etc.), producing pus and discharge, foul smell, and low appetite. Treatment: inject Prostaglandin twice, 11–14 days apart, to open the cervix and trigger contractions that expel infected material (Oxytocin doesn't work here, since it can't 'open' the uterus and only triggers contraction during actual delivery); inject antibiotics (Tetracycline or Tylosin) for 5 days; do not flush the uterus with iodine or permanganate solution, since this irritates it and a large fluid volume impairs the uterus returning to normal size. Prevention: cows that had a difficult delivery needing manual assistance, a retained placenta, or post-delivery mastitis are at higher risk — give Prostaglandin 24 hours after delivery and again 2 weeks later. Anoestrus: a non-pregnant cow not coming into heat, which is normal in the early phase of nursing a calf; causes of prolonged/abnormal anoestrus include poor body condition (suppresses cycling), ongoing calf suckling, and cystic ovaries. Treatment: proper feeding and timely weaning restores normal cycling; for luteal cysts in an otherwise well-conditioned animal, 5 ml Prostaglandin (Lutalyse) induces estrus within 3–5 days. Repeat breeding: normal 3-week heat cycles but failure to conceive after 3 or more services with confirmed true estrus. Causes: endometritis (bacterial uterine infection after delivery preventing normal embryo development — sometimes hard to diagnose since cattle don't always visibly discharge pus) or a sterile bull (worth switching bulls for the next service if suspected). Treatment: Prostaglandin twice, 11–14 days apart, plus antibiotics (Tetracycline or Tylosin) for 5 days.
